abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel theoretical framework that fundamentally reconceptualizes how causality is understood in empirical software engineering research. Traditional approaches to establishing causal relationships in software metrics have relied primarily on correlational analyses, which fail to account for the complex feedback mechanisms inherent in software development processes. We introduce the Causal Software Engineering Loop (CSEL), a theoretical model grounded in complex adaptive systems theory that explicates how development practices, quality outcomes, and team dynamics mutually influence each other over time. Through rigorous mathematical formalization, we demonstrate how traditional statistical methods systematically misinterpret directionality in software data due to their inability to handle recursive causation. The framework introduces three novel constructs—feedback strength coefficients, temporal lag distributions, and emergent quality thresholds—that enable researchers to model software phenomena as dynamic systems rather than static relationships. We validate the framework's explanatory power through re-analysis of three landmark defect prediction studies, revealing that previously accepted conclusions about tool effectiveness were artifacts of causal misspecification. This paradigm shift in theoretical understanding has profound implications for research methodology, suggesting that empirical software engineering must adopt systems-thinking approaches to avoid systematic bias in our understanding of how software practices influence outcomes. The CSEL framework opens new avenues for studying software processes as interconnected ecosystems rather than isolated variables.

Software cost estimation remains one of the most challenging problems in software engineering, with significant implications for project planning and resource allocation. While numerous estimation models have been proposed, existing theoretical foundations fail to adequately account for the heterogeneous nature of software development contexts. This paper advances the theoretical basis for effort estimation by extending the Constructive Cost Model (COCOMO) through the integration of contextual contingency theory. We propose the Contextual Effort Estimation Model (CEEM), which introduces dynamic adjustment factors that respond to project-specific characteristics rather than applying uniform assumptions across diverse development environments. The theoretical contribution lies in our formal analysis of how contextual variables interact with base effort equations, demonstrating that traditional parametric models systematically underestimate effort variability by assuming homogeneous sensitivity to cost drivers. We derive mathematically rigorous relationships between organizational maturity, team composition, and technology familiarity that improve upon COCOMO's linear scaling assumptions. Our theoretical extensions incorporate insights from organizational learning theory to explain how estimation accuracy improves through repeated calibration cycles. The model introduces composite adjustment vectors that capture the non-linear interactions between project scale and contextual complexity. Validation through systematic comparison with historical project data demonstrates that CEEM's theoretical improvements yield measurable gains in estimation accuracy, particularly for large-scale distributed development efforts where contextual heterogeneity is most pronounced. This work provides both a theoretical advancement and practical guidance for improving estimation practice.

The exponential growth in software repository data has created unprecedented opportunities for empirical research, yet existing analysis tools fail to capture the multi-dimensional nature of software development phenomena. This paper introduces DEEPANALYTICS, a novel distributed computing platform designed specifically for holistic mining of software repositories that transcends the limitations of single-repository analysis tools. Unlike existing approaches that treat version control, issue tracking, code review, and communication channels as isolated data sources, DEEPANALYTICS implements a unified temporal graph model that represents the complex interdependencies between these artifacts. The system's architecture employs a custom streaming computation model optimized for time-series analysis of developer behavior patterns, enabling researchers to trace the complete lifecycle of software decisions from initial conception through implementation to maintenance. We present three innovative technical contributions: (1) a cross-repository entity resolution algorithm that links developer identities across different project platforms, (2) a real-time anomaly detection subsystem for identifying unusual coordination patterns, and (3) a natural language interface that enables researchers without programming expertise to formulate complex temporal queries. The system's evaluation demonstrates its ability to uncover previously invisible patterns in how geographically distributed teams coordinate work, revealing that communication latency artifacts in issue tracking systems serve as leading indicators of integration failures. DEEPANALYTICS represents a paradigm shift in how the research community conducts empirical studies of software development, enabling longitudinal analyses at scales previously infeasible while maintaining analytical rigor.

Automated defect prediction has demonstrated significant potential for improving software quality, yet practical adoption remains limited due to the brittleness of existing tools when confronted with the characteristic distribution shifts that occur between training and deployment contexts. This paper presents ADAPTDEFECT, an enhanced defect prediction system that substantially improves upon current approaches through a novel continuous learning architecture designed to handle real-world concept drift. While prior systems rely on static models trained once and deployed indefinitely, ADAPTDEFECT implements a hierarchical adaptation framework that dynamically recalibrates prediction thresholds based on incoming validation feedback. The system's core innovation lies in its hybrid ensemble strategy that combines stability-oriented base classifiers with volatility-sensitive drift detectors, enabling the system to distinguish genuine distribution shifts from normal noise without requiring manual intervention. We substantially improved upon existing visualization approaches by developing an interactive diagnostic dashboard that helps practitioners understand why predictions change over time, addressing the interpretability concerns that have hindered practitioner adoption. The technical architecture incorporates incremental learning algorithms optimized for imbalanced class distributions common in defect datasets, achieving sustained predictive performance across multiple release cycles without complete model retraining. Empirical evaluation on four industrial datasets spanning 18 months of continuous operation demonstrates that ADAPTDEFECT achieves a 34% improvement in sustained F1 score compared to state-of-the-art approaches, while reducing the average time between concept drift detection and model adaptation from days to minutes. This work provides both a substantially improved prediction system and empirical evidence that continuous adaptation is essential for practical defect prediction deployment.
